newsitem.title: USA: Capital decline triggers Home Insurance action.
newsitem.headline: Capital decline triggers Home Insurance action.

text.p: New Hampshire insurance regulators placed Home Insurance Co under formal supervision on Tuesday after a troubling decline in the company's capital, an insurance department representative said.
The order of supervision places tighter controls on the Home, but falls short of an outright takeover, or receivership, by the New Hampshire insurance department, representative David Nichols said.

The Home, the principal subsidiary of Home Holdings Inc, ceased writing new business in June 1995 and was placed into runoff. Since then it has been actively monitored by the New Hampshire insurance department, the Home's principal regulator.

Sweden's Trygg-Hansa/SPP Holding AB is a majority shareholder of Home Holdings and Zurich Insurance Co has an equity position and warrants to purchase more, Nichols said. Both are controlling parties of the Home.
Nichols said Trygg-Hansa and Zurich are not required to invest any more in the Home.
But the New Hampshire insurance department was forced to take mandatory control of the Home after its risk-based capital fell below certain required levels, Nichols said.
Risk-based capital is a measure of a company's assets and liabilities used by regulators to determine financial strength.
The Home's cash flow was not an issue, Nichols said.
The Home's financial deterioration renewed the concerns of some in the industry about a similar transaction by CIGNA Corp.
CIGNA last year split its domestic property-casualty business into one company for the ongoing profitable business and a separate, runoff company for the unprofitable, discontinued business.
Critics of that restructuring have expressed concern the runoff operation may not have enough capital to pay future claims.
But Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Weston Hicks said he believes the two transactions are different because CIGNA is a strong parent that has said it will stand behind its runoff operation.

The rapid deterioration of the Home's financial condition, however, may keep other insurance companies from taking similar steps to move their unprofitable asbestos and environmental liabilities into a separate runoff operation, Hicks said.
Two separate studies of the Home's core reserves and asbestos and environmental liabilities are still ongoing, Nichols said.

The company's initial study by the Milliman & Robertson actuarial firm was begun about a year ago. The insurance department in January retained a second actuarial firm, Tillinghast to do a separate review, Nichols said.
He could not project when the studies might be completed, but he said the department's action was not in response to those studies.
